title: Dimensions and Scaling
description: Dimension-theoretic vocabulary covering multiple non-equivalent notions of dimension in combinatorial, fractal, and disordered geometry, along with scaling regimes and diffusion exponents.

hausdorff-dimension.summary: A measure-theoretic dimension defined by the asymptotic behavior of covers by sets of small diameter; can be non-integer for fractal sets.
hausdorff-dimension.definition:
A **measure-theoretic dimension** defined by examining the asymptotic behavior of covers by sets of small diameter:

$$\dim_H(S) = \inf \{s \geq 0 : H^s(S) = 0\}$$

where $H^s$ is the $s$-dimensional Hausdorff measure. This is the most refined notion of dimension for general sets — agrees with the topological dimension on smooth manifolds but can be non-integer.

examples.title: Smooth manifold
examples.body: For a smooth $n$-dimensional manifold, the Hausdorff dimension equals the topological dimension $n$.

examples.title: Cantor set
examples.body: The middle-thirds Cantor set has Hausdorff dimension $\log 2 / \log 3 \approx 0.631$, which is non-integer.

formulas.description: Hausdorff dimension defined as the critical exponent at which the Hausdorff measure transitions from infinity to zero.

variables.S: The set whose dimension is being measured

fractal-dimension.summary: The non-integer dimension of a self-similar set, computed from the number and scale of self-similar copies.
fractal-dimension.definition:
The general term for **non-integer dimensions of self-similar sets**. For a set composed of $N$ scaled copies of itself, each at scale $1/s$:

$$d_f = \frac{\log N}{\log s}$$

This is the **similarity dimension**, agreeing with Hausdorff dimension under reasonable conditions (Moran's theorem).

examples.title: Sierpiński gasket
examples.body: The Sierpiński gasket is composed of $N=3$ copies at scale $1/s = 1/2$, giving $d_f = \log 3 / \log 2 \approx 1.585$.

examples.title: Koch snowflake
examples.body: The Koch curve is composed of $N=4$ copies at scale $1/s = 1/3$, giving $d_f = \log 4 / \log 3 \approx 1.262$.

formulas.description: Similarity dimension for a self-similar set made of N copies each scaled by factor 1/s.

variables.s: Scaling factor (each copy has linear size 1/s of the original)

box-counting-dimension.summary: Dimension defined by counting the minimum number of boxes of side ε needed to cover a set, as ε → 0.
box-counting-dimension.definition:
Defined via counts of $\epsilon$-boxes needed to cover a set:

$$\dim_{\text{box}}(S) = \lim_{\epsilon \to 0} \frac{\log N(\epsilon)}{\log(1/\epsilon)}$$

where $N(\epsilon)$ is the minimum number of boxes of side $\epsilon$. Easier to compute than Hausdorff but equal for 'nice' sets.

examples.title: Smooth curve
examples.body: A smooth curve in the plane requires $O(1/\epsilon)$ boxes of side $\epsilon$, giving $\dim_{\text{box}} = 1$.

formulas.description: Box-counting dimension as the limiting log-ratio of box count to inverse box size.

variables.N(\\epsilon): Minimum number of boxes of side ε needed to cover S

effective-dimension.summary: The exponent governing the polynomial growth of BFS balls on a graph; the primary geometric dimension used in the project.
effective-dimension.definition:
Also called **connectivity dimension**, this is the exponent governing the **growth of breadth-first-search (BFS) balls**:

$$V(r) = |\{v : d(v, v_0) \leq r\}| \sim r^{d_{\text{eff}}}$$

as $r \to \infty$ on an infinite graph. For $\mathbb{Z}^n$: $d_{\text{eff}} = n$. For random graphs near percolation: $d_{\text{eff}}$ can be non-integer.

This is the project's primary geometric dimension — what the graph 'looks like' from far away.

examples.title: Integer lattice
examples.body: On $\mathbb{Z}^n$, the BFS ball of radius $r$ contains $\Theta(r^n)$ vertices, so $d_{\text{eff}} = n$.

examples.title: Percolation cluster
examples.body: Near the percolation threshold, the incipient infinite cluster has $d_{\text{eff}}$ that can be non-integer, reflecting the fractal geometry of the cluster.

formulas.description: Volume growth of BFS balls defining the effective dimension.

variables.V(r): Number of vertices within graph distance r of a base vertex v_0

connectivity-dimension.summary: Synonym for effective dimension, emphasizing that it depends only on the combinatorial structure of the graph.
connectivity-dimension.definition:
Synonym for **effective dimension**. The term emphasizes that it depends only on the **combinatorial structure** of the graph, not on any Euclidean embedding.

See **Effective Dimension** for the full definition and formulas.

power-law-growth.summary: The scaling V(r) ~ r^d that defines the effective dimension, extracted via log-log regression.
power-law-growth.definition:
The scaling $V(r) \sim r^d$ that **defines** the effective dimension. The exponent $d$ is extracted via a **log-log fit** of $V(r)$ vs $r$:

$$\log V(r) \approx d \log r + \text{const}$$

This is the fundamental empirical method for estimating combinatorial dimensions from graph data.

examples.title: Log-log regression
examples.body: Given BFS ball sizes $V(1), V(2), \ldots, V(R)$, plot $\log V(r)$ vs $\log r$ and fit a line. The slope estimates $d_{\text{eff}}$.

formulas.description: Log-log linearization of power-law volume growth used to extract the effective dimension by linear regression.

variables.V(r): BFS ball volume at radius r

walk-dimension.summary: The exponent d_w in the mean-squared displacement ⟨Δx²⟩ ~ t^(2/d_w) of a random walker on a graph.
walk-dimension.definition:
The exponent in **mean-squared displacement** of a random walker on the graph:

$$\langle \Delta x^2 \rangle \sim t^{2/d_w}$$

For ordinary Brownian motion on $\mathbb{R}^n$ or a regular lattice: $d_w = 2$. On fractals and disordered graphs, $d_w$ can deviate.

- $d_w > 2$: **sub-diffusion** (walker trapped by geometric bottlenecks)
- $d_w < 2$: **super-diffusion** (ballistic propagation)
- $d_w = 2$: ordinary Brownian diffusion

examples.title: Regular lattice
examples.body: On $\mathbb{Z}^n$, random walks satisfy $\langle \Delta x^2 \rangle \sim t$, so $d_w = 2$.

examples.title: Sierpiński gasket
examples.body: On the Sierpiński gasket, $d_w \approx 2.32 > 2$, reflecting sub-diffusion caused by the fractal geometry.

formulas.description: Mean-squared displacement scaling defining the walk dimension.

variables.\\langle \\Delta x^2 \\rangle: Mean-squared displacement of the random walker

sub-diffusion.summary: Diffusion slower than Brownian motion, characterized by d_w > 2, caused by geometric bottlenecks trapping the walker.
sub-diffusion.definition:
Diffusion **slower than Brownian**, i.e., $d_w > 2$. The walker is 'trapped' by geometric bottlenecks. Common on fractals (e.g., Sierpiński gasket has $d_w \approx 2.32$).

In the project context, the sheet structure of pentagonal tilings may cause sub-diffusion if vortices trap walkers that wind around them multiple times.

examples.title: Sierpiński gasket
examples.body: The Sierpiński gasket has $d_w \approx 2.32$, so $\langle \Delta x^2 \rangle \sim t^{2/2.32} \approx t^{0.86}$, growing slower than linear.

super-diffusion.summary: Diffusion faster than Brownian motion, characterized by d_w < 2, due to long-range correlations enabling ballistic propagation.
super-diffusion.definition: Diffusion **faster than Brownian**, $d_w < 2$. The walker propagates ballistically due to long-range correlations. Rare on graphs with bounded degree but possible in special settings.

mean-squared-displacement.summary: The expected squared distance ⟨(X_t − X_0)²⟩ traveled by a random walker in t steps; its log-log slope gives 2/d_w.
mean-squared-displacement.definition:
The quantity

$$\langle \Delta x^2 \rangle_t = \mathbb{E}[(X_t - X_0)^2]$$

measured along a random walk. The slope of its log-log fit is $2/d_w$.

examples.title: Brownian motion
examples.body: For standard Brownian motion on $\mathbb{R}^n$, $\langle \Delta x^2 \rangle_t = nt$, giving a log-log slope of 1, consistent with $d_w = 2$.

formulas.description: Mean squared displacement of a random walk at time t.

variables.X_t: Position of the random walker at time t
variables.X_0: Initial position of the random walker

anomalous-diffusion.summary: Diffusion with d_w ≠ 2; the general phenomenon of random walks on fractals and complex networks deviating from classical Brownian scaling.
anomalous-diffusion.definition:
**Diffusion with $d_w \neq 2$**. The general phenomenon that random walks on fractals and complex networks deviate from the classical Brownian scaling.

Encompasses both sub-diffusion ($d_w > 2$) and super-diffusion ($d_w < 2$).

examples.title: Fractal lattices
examples.body: Random walks on the Sierpiński gasket, percolation clusters, and other fractal structures all exhibit anomalous diffusion with $d_w \neq 2$.

spectral-dimension.summary: The exponent d_spec in the return probability P_0(t) ~ t^(−d_spec/2) of a random walk; also governs the low-energy density of states of the graph Laplacian.
spectral-dimension.definition:
The exponent in the **return probability** of a random walk:

$$P_0(t) = \text{Prob}[X_t = X_0] \sim t^{-d_{\text{spec}}/2}$$

For Brownian motion on $\mathbb{R}^n$: $d_{\text{spec}} = n$. For fractals, $d_{\text{spec}}$ can be non-integer and is often **smaller than $d_{\text{eff}}$**.

The spectral dimension also governs the **low-energy density of states** of the graph Laplacian:

$$\rho(\lambda) \sim \lambda^{d_{\text{spec}}/2 - 1} \quad \text{as } \lambda \to 0$$

examples.title: Regular lattice
examples.body: On $\mathbb{Z}^n$, the return probability decays as $P_0(t) \sim t^{-n/2}$, so $d_{\text{spec}} = n = d_{\text{eff}}$.

examples.title: Causal Dynamical Triangulation
examples.body: In CDT quantum gravity, $d_{\text{spec}} \to 2$ in the UV and $d_{\text{spec}} \to 4$ in the IR, demonstrating dimensional flow.

formulas.description: Return probability of a random walk defining the spectral dimension.

variables.P_0(t): Probability that the random walker returns to its starting point after t steps

formulas.description: Low-energy density of states of the graph Laplacian governed by the spectral dimension.

variables.\\rho(\\lambda): Density of states of the graph Laplacian at eigenvalue λ

alexander-orbach-relation.summary: The fundamental identity d_spec = 2·d_eff / d_w relating the three combinatorial dimensions; a key diagnostic consistency check.
alexander-orbach-relation.definition:
A fundamental identity tying the three combinatorial dimensions together:

$$d_{\text{spec}} = \frac{2 d_{\text{eff}}}{d_w}$$

This relation holds for random walks on a wide class of homogeneous fractals and graphs. Consequences:

- If $d_w = 2$ (ordinary diffusion): $d_{\text{spec}} = d_{\text{eff}}$.
- If $d_w > 2$ (sub-diffusion): $d_{\text{spec}} < d_{\text{eff}}$.
- $d_w < 2$ (super-diffusion): $d_{\text{spec}} > d_{\text{eff}}$.

The Alexander–Orbach relation is one of the project's key diagnostic tools: knowing any two dimensions determines the third, providing consistency checks for numerical estimates.

examples.title: Regular lattice consistency check
examples.body: On $\mathbb{Z}^n$: $d_{\text{eff}} = n$, $d_w = 2$, $d_{\text{spec}} = n$. Check: $2n/2 = n$. ✓

examples.title: Sub-diffusive fractal
examples.body: If $d_{\text{eff}} = 2$ and $d_w = 2.5$, then $d_{\text{spec}} = 2 \cdot 2 / 2.5 = 1.6 < 2$, indicating dimensional reduction relative to the effective dimension.

formulas.description: Alexander–Orbach relation connecting spectral, effective, and walk dimensions.

uv-regime.summary: The short-distance / short-time scaling regime that probes the microscopic structure of the graph.
uv-regime.definition:
The **short-distance / short-time regime**:

- Small spatial separation.
- Short walk times.
- Large momentum / high frequency in Fourier picture.
- Probes the **microscopic structure** of the graph (individual tiles, local connectivity).

The UV and IR can have **different effective dimensions** — a phenomenon called **dimensional flow**.

examples.title: CDT quantum gravity
examples.body: In Causal Dynamical Triangulation, the UV regime has $d_{\text{spec}} \approx 2$, reflecting the microscopic 2D structure of the triangulation.

ir-regime.summary: The long-distance / long-time scaling regime that probes the macroscopic and emergent structure of the graph.
ir-regime.definition:
The **long-distance / long-time regime**:

- Large spatial separation.
- Long walk times.
- Small momentum / low frequency.
- Probes **macroscopic** / **emergent** structure.

The UV and IR can have **different effective dimensions** — a phenomenon called **dimensional flow**.

examples.title: CDT quantum gravity
examples.body: In Causal Dynamical Triangulation, the IR regime has $d_{\text{spec}} \approx 4$, recovering the expected 4D macroscopic spacetime.

dimensional-flow.summary: Scale-dependent effective dimension: the dimension observed depends on the length or time scale of observation, with UV and IR values potentially differing.
dimensional-flow.definition:
**Scale-dependent dimension**: the effective dimension depends on the length/time scale of observation. The UV value differs from the IR value.

Examples:

- Causal Dynamical Triangulation: $d_{\text{spec}} \to 2$ in UV, $d_{\text{spec}} \to 4$ in IR.
- Asymptotic safety: similar UV $\to$ IR running.
- Pentagonal tilings (in the project): possibly $d_{\text{spec}}$ flow between $\sim 1.5$ and $\sim 2$.

Dimensional flow can be visualized as a plot of 'local slope' of log-log data, showing how the apparent exponent runs with scale.

examples.title: CDT quantum gravity
examples.body: In CDT, the spectral dimension flows from $d_{\text{spec}} \approx 2$ at short scales (UV) to $d_{\text{spec}} \approx 4$ at large scales (IR), matching the observed 4D macroscopic universe.

examples.title: Pentagonal tilings
examples.body: The multi-sheeted pentagonal tilings in the project may exhibit $d_{\text{spec}}$ flow between approximately 1.5 and 2, providing a discrete combinatorial echo of quantum gravity's dimensional flow.

dimensional-reduction.summary: A specific form of dimensional flow where the effective dimension decreases at short scales (UV), observed in CDT, asymptotic safety, and holography.
dimensional-reduction.definition:
A specific form of dimensional flow where the **effective dimension decreases at long scales** or in the UV. Observed in:

- CDT quantum gravity: 4D macroscopic, ~2D microscopic.
- Asymptotic safety: 2D UV fixed point.
- Holographic renormalization: bulk dimension reduces to boundary dimension at IR.

The conjecture is that **graphs with non-trivial topology** (sheet structure) can naturally exhibit dimensional reduction, providing a discrete model of quantum-gravity behavior.

examples.title: CDT quantum gravity
examples.body: CDT simulations show the spectral dimension dropping from 4 (IR) to approximately 2 (UV), suggesting that spacetime becomes effectively 2-dimensional at the Planck scale.

examples.title: Pentagonal multi-sheeted tilings
examples.body: If the sheet structure causes sub-diffusion ($d_w > 2$), then by Alexander–Orbach, $d_{\text{spec}} < 2$, mimicking dimensional reduction in a purely combinatorial setting.

universality-class.summary: A set of systems sharing the same scaling exponents (d_eff, d_w, d_spec) and critical scaling laws, independent of microscopic details.
universality-class.definition:
A **set of systems sharing scaling exponents** — i.e., having the same $d_{\text{eff}}$, $d_w$, $d_{\text{spec}}$ and the same critical scaling laws. Universality means microscopic details don't matter for large-scale behavior; only symmetry, dimension, and range of interaction matter.

The **renormalization group** formalizes this: a universality class is a fixed point of the RG flow.

examples.title: Ising universality class
examples.body: The 2D Ising model and many other systems with $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry in 2D share the same critical exponents, forming a universality class.

examples.title: Percolation universality class
examples.body: Random bond percolation and site percolation on different 2D lattices share the same fractal dimension and scaling exponents at the critical threshold.
